claims.text: A model that separately calculates lattice and electronic heat transport can predict the total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr within ±10% over 50–1200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits a crossover near 200 K from lattice-dominated transport to a significant electronic contribution.
Powder metallurgy and hot isostatic pressing will produce homogeneous, near-equilibrium, defect-minimized HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
The specimens will have controlled oxygen content below 1 wt.%.
The computational framework will combine full-spectrum ab initio phonon calculations that do not require a Debye-temperature approximation with Boltzmann electronic-transport calculations.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The absence of significant defect clusters or phase segregation preserves intrinsic phonon- and electron-scattering behavior.
Separating phonon-mediated and electron-mediated heat transport improves predictive performance.
Earlier models conflated lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions.
Earlier models relied on oversimplified Debye approximations.
Full-spectrum phonon dispersion and electron-scattering-rate calculations accurately predict the temperature dependence of the two transport channels.
The new model will reduce the thermal-conductivity prediction error by roughly 20–30% relative to earlier approaches.
Below approximately 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions will be nearly equal.
Above approximately 200 K, the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution becomes increasingly significant.
Earlier computational and analytical approaches typically deviated from experimental conductivity measurements by 20–30%.
The prediction is applicable to refractory high-entropy alloys having minimal extrinsic defects and secondary phases.
High oxygen content can create oxide precipitates that limit the model's applicability.
The model may cease to be valid in regimes where anharmonic effects dominate.
Electron–phonon separation is especially uncertain at approximately 200–300 K.
Variation in real-sample microstructure can cause prediction errors greater than ±10%.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls low-temperature transport lattice-dominated, whereas the conditions and predicted outcome describe the lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K as comparable or nearly equal.

The falsification rule refers to a crossover in the dominant mechanism near 200 K, but the main prediction only says that the electronic contribution becomes significant or increasingly significant above 200 K; it does not clearly predict electronic dominance.
